newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-CUT OUT THE ROUGH STUFF, SAYS COACH.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-CUT OUT THE ROUGH STUFF, SAYS COACH.

text.p: Canada coach Andy Murray has instructed his players to cut out some of the rough stuff when they play Sweden in the second game of the ice hockey world championship final on Tuesday.
The Canadians were their own worst enemies on Sunday as Sweden scored two powerplay goals on the way to a 3-2 win in the opening game of the best-of-three gold medal final.
After an equally indisciplined 7-2 loss to the Swedes during round-robin play, Murray had hoped his team had learned their lesson.
But he was forced to admit after Sunday's defeat that the message had not completely sunk in.
"We took some unnecessary penalties but I think we learned quite a bit from last time...the score was closer," said Murray.

The Swedes have been able to bring out the nastiness in the Canadians at this championship and that ability as much as their slick passing and smooth skating has the Olympic champions one win away from adding a seventh world title to their collection.
Sweden are bracing themselves for an all-out assault by the Canadians on Tuesday as they look to extend the final series to third game.
"I think they will attack even more then they have," said Niklas Sundblad. "They have to, they're forced to win."

The Canadians blamed their first defeat by Sweden and any other difficulties they have encountered here to adjusting to the European game and officiating. Their complaints have been loud and plentiful.
But they have only themselves to blame for the hole they find themselves in, even Murray admitting the penalties they picked up against Sweden were warranted.
"We try to tell our players how important discipline is, we emphasise that all the time," said Murray, frustrated that the message has yet to sink in.
"It's just hard for these players because the game is called differently over here.
"But I told Jeff Friesen and Cory Cross that the penalties they took at the end of the game would have been penalties in any league.
"The problem is that when you're in a playoff game in the NHL you want to make a physical impression on the other team. That's not possible here.
In fact, the Swedes have shown no sign of being phased by the physical Canadian game.
They are big, strong and appear to relish the heavy traffic along the boards that they once avoided. On occasions the Swedes have gone out of their way to look for trouble.
